description.narrative: Projektet YEE AET Zambia har som mål att öka antalet jobb för unga människor, särskilt unga kvinnor, inom livsmedelsindustrin och bidra till företagsutveckling genom ökad handel i Zambia. De specifika målen är att: (1) Öka handelsmöjligheterna för unga människor, även inom klimatresilienta livsmedelsvärdekedjor; (2) Öka ungas tillgång till formella anställningsmöjligheter; och (3) förbättra stödet för ökad jämställdhet och inkludering av ungdomar genom policyramverk. Projektets slutmål är att bidra till att öka sysselsättnings-, entreprenörs- och handelsmöjligheterna så att unga zambiska män och kvinnor får bättre och mer motståndskraftiga försörjningsmöjligheter.

The YEE AET Zambia project aims to increase jobs for young people, particularly young women, in the agri-food industry and contribute to enterprise growth through increased trade in Zambia. The specific objectives are to: (1) Increase trading opportunities for young people, also in climate resilient in high value agri-food value-chains; (2) Increase young people access to decent (self) employment; and (3) Improve policy support and market decisions for increased gender equality and youth inclusion. The end goal of the project is to contribute to increase the employment, entrepreneurial and trade opportunities so that young Zambian men and women have better and more resilient livelihoods.

title.narrative: SNV Youth Employment and Entrepreneurship AET Zambia
SNV Youth Employment and Entrepreneurship AET Zambia

description.narrative:
Results from 2025 annual report:
The annual report demonstrates some implementation progress of the SNV Youth Employment and Entrepreneurship AET Zambia 2024-2028 during 2025, particularly regarding youth skills development and enterprise creation. Across the programme, 21,074 youth completed life, financial and business skills training (SNV YEE AET Annual Report 2025, p. 22)., and 1,918 new and graduated youth enterprises have been established (SNV YEE AET Annual Report 2025, p. 4). Worth noting though is that these results are for the entire program, with results aggregated for both Zambia and Zimbabwe.
For the case of specific results for Zambia, the report demonstrates progress in enterprise development, skills training, employment creation and access to productive resources. One of the most significant results was the establishment of 1,692 youth-led enterprises in Zambia across value chains including legumes, honey production, poultry, fish farming, goats and piggery (SNV YEE AET Annual Report 2025, pp. 17-18). The report further notes that 26 per cent of Zambian enterprises are already employing additional workers, suggesting early evidence of business growth and job creation beyond self-employment (p. 20). These results indicate that programme-supported youth enterprises are increasingly participating in market-oriented value chains and creating broader economic opportunities.
A second important result was the strengthening of youth access to markets and private-sector partnerships. Twenty-three private-sector firms in Zambia entered into structured collaboration with the programme, including Good Nature Agro, Seed Co, Sun King, Vision Fund Zambia, Jacaranda Hub and Kansanshi Mine Foundation (SNV YEE AET Annual Report 2025, p. 19). These partnerships provide internships, employment opportunities, access to productive assets, financial services, technical expertise and market linkages. Notably, the partnership with Good Nature Agro engaged approximately 1,600 youth in soya bean contract farming arrangements, demonstrating how private-sector actors are increasingly contributing to youth economic inclusion (p. 20).
The programme also achieved substantial results in youth skills development. In Zambia, 16,286 youth completed life, financial and business skills training (p. 22), while 4,139 youth completed technical and vocational training in areas such as leather processing, crop production, livestock management, agroforestry and agribusiness development (p. 24).
The report further demonstrates promising institutional and systems-level results. In Zambia, the YEE Basic Skills Curriculum was reviewed and approved by the Technical Education, Vocational and Entrepreneurship Training Authority (TEVETA). Youth who complete the training will now be eligible to receive a TEVETAaccredited certificate, enhancing the recognition of their skills and strengthening their prospects for both employment and entrepreneurship (SNV YEE AET Annual Report 2025, p. 23) but also creating opportunities for institutionalisation and future scaling of the training model.
The programme further contributed to improved financial inclusion among young people. By the end of 2025, 6,356 Zambian youth were participating in Youth Savings and Lending Associations (YSALs), collectively generating savings of USD 76,567 and accessing loans worth USD 60,068 (p. 27). The report highlights that these mechanisms help youth develop savings habits, financial management skills and creditworthiness, creating pathways towards formal financial services.
The programme also contributed to improved access to productive resources. Through engagement with traditional leaders and local authorities, 123 acres of land were allocated to 325 youth for productive activities linked to horticulture and agroforestry enterprises (SNV YEE AET Annual Report 2025, p. 30). This represents an important change among local stakeholders and traditional authorities, who are increasingly recognising youth as economic actors and supporting youth access to productive assets.
The programme also strengthened youth participation in policy and advocacy processes. In Zambia, youth also participated in policy dialogue platforms, including the YEE Project Advisory Board, the Youth Socio-Economic Empowerment Community of Practice and the National Youth Indaba (SNV YEE AET Annual Report 2025, p. 31). Furthermore, programme-supported advocacy contributed to the revision of gender- and social inclusion-sensitive by-laws within the Chamuka Royal Establishment, following commitments by traditional leaders to promote equitable access to land and resources for women and youth (p. 32). These developments suggest increasing ownership and responsiveness among institutional actors regarding youth economic empowerment.
Overall, the results achieved during 2025 demonstrate meaningful progress in Zambia. At the same time, Sida notes that progress remains uneven across outcome areas and that the pace of implementation may pose challenges for achieving all intended programme targets within the remaining implementation period, particularly given the reduction of the programme duration by 14 months. The Embassy will therefore continue to follow progress closely, especially during the upcoming results harvesting exercise.
